latin: Non intellego! Cujus horae dimidia est?
Nescio! Tantum scio dimidiam esse: acus minor horologio meo deest.
Heri sexta<sup>2</sup> hora et dimidia Lutetiam reliqui<sup>3</sup>.
Lugdunum hodie tertia hora postmeridiana<sup>4</sup> relinquo.
In hanc urbem adveni decima hora et quinta decima minuta, id est decima hora et quadrante<sup>5</sup>.
Manes Lugduni quattuor horas et quadraginta quinque minutas.
Nobis est otium: visne<sup>6</sup> mecum<sup>7</sup> prandere? Ecce popina!
Relinquo, relinquis, relinquit, relinquimus, relinquitis, relinquunt, relinquere. Reliqui, reliquisti, reliquit, reliquimus, reliquistis, reliquerunt, reliquisse.
english: What time is it (how-many-eth hour is)?
It is the half hour (half hour is)…
I do not understand! Of what hour [is it the half] (half is)?
I don’t know! I only know [it is the half hour] (half to-be): the small hand is missing from my watch (needle smaller to-clock mine is-lacking).
I left Paris yesterday at six thirty (yesterday at-the-sixth hour and at-the-half Paris I-left).
I leave Lyon today at three o’clock p.m. (Lyon today at-third hour afternoonian I-leave).
I arrived in this city at ten fifteen (To this city I-arrived at-tenth hour and at-fifth tenth minute), i.e. (that is) at a quarter past ten (at-tenth hour and at-quarter).
You are staying in Lyon four hours and forty-five minutes.
We have time (to-us is leisure): do you want to lunch with me? Here-is (behold) a restaurant!
Excellent! I’m really hungry (strongly I-am-hungry). Let’s go to the restaurant.
I leave, you leave, etc., they leave, to leave. I (have) left, you (have)…, etc., they (have) left, to have left.

footnotes: Quota is an adjective which agrees with hora.

Sexta hora and not sex horae, because it is the sixth hour (see note number 6 in the previous lesson). But further down (P 9) quattuor horas because this time it is four hours forming together a certain interval of time.

Reliqui is a perfect (tense corresponding to the English simple past, I left, and also the English present perfect tense, I have left). Simply note, in phrase 12, the differences between the present and the perfect tense.
Postmeridianá, just as dimidiá, is an adjective: it agrees therefore with horá, hence the long quantity of the á which indicates here the form of the adverbial phrase.
Quadrante; if this word were the subject, we would have quadrans. It means: a quarter of an as, the as being a currency; and hence quarter of a circle (Eng.: quadrant), whence quarter of an hour.
Visne = vis + ne, interrogative particle which should know well by now. The verb volo, I want, is irregular: we will see it again soon.
Mecum = cum me, with me; we also have tecum, with you; nobiscum, with us; vobiscum, with you(pl.).

Adeamus, let us go! adimus, we go. The former is a subjunctive, a mood very often used in Latin, but of which we will only see the conjugation later on. The latter is the present indicative, which is conjugated as follows: adeo, adis, adit, adimus, aditis, adeunt.

This verb is irregular (cf. L 5, N 3), just as is the verb eo from which it is compounded by the addition of the preposition ad, towards. Regular verbs ending in -eo in the first person remain in e in all the others. Thus video, I see, gives: vides, videt, videmus, videtis, vident.
comments: N.B. In phrase 4 one could have said index instead of acus.

latin: Navis oneraria sexta decima hora et quinquagesima minuta portum reliquit.
Mihi est otium: Lutetiam videre volo.
english: The freighter left port at four fifty (16:50).
If you are hungry, we can go to a restaurant.
I’m at leisure: I want to see Paris.
When did you leave the restaurant?
I left it at ten pm (22:00).
You drank many glasses of wine.
Not at all, I only drank coffee.
